fullText:
new blog post by me, "The Harsh Geometry of Superintelligence--  The Selfish Supermind Attractor Generally Has a Wider Basin than the BGI Attractor"

https://t.co/HnUTwymq0Q

So ... in a series of prequel posts I have described several kinds of possible AGI mind, each with its own basic drives and each tending --  as it increases its intelligence and capability, to stay roughly the kind it starts out as..

Examples are: 

* the power-seeking maximizer of Steve Omohundro’s 2008 "Basic AI Drives" paper

* the BGI minds that my colleagues and I are trying to build, ...and half a dozen others.

Knowing what kinds of superintelligent minds are attractors under intelligence/capability increase  is only part of the puzzle, though. 

The next question is: What are the shapes of the basins of these attractors?

I.e, the zillion-dollar (actually, well, money-obsoleting…) question is: Which kind of attractor will a given early-stage AGI system fall into and how hard will it be to knock out again? 

In dynamical systems terms, this depends on how wide and how deep the basin around each one is.

So this blog post analyzes these attractor basins a bit, with an aim toward milking lessons for building AGI systems and for understanding what an AGI system should do when something strange happens to it that may potentially zoink it out of its historical attractor basin. 

The disturbing yet unsurprising punchline here is: While Omohundro’s original “Basic AI Drives” paper overstated the omnipresence of the “selfish” attractor in the space of superminds … nonetheless it DOES seem that the selfish attractor has a big, wide and deep basin that makes it especially easy for AGI systems to fall into it … if they are not designed just right….

This doesn’t mean you need some sort of extremely carefully calibrated mathematical design to avoid convergence to selfishness – but it does mean that if you don’t bother to build things like compassion and goal-continuity into your AI system’s initial goal framework, you have no reason to expect your system to converge elsewhere than to a selfish Omohundro-esque attractor as it self-modifies and its intelligence and capability increase.

Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.
